readerTitle: Same pricing switch, two very different months
caseNote: 가상 사례 (공유 주방, 이미지 처리 소프트웨어, 바닥 청소기 제조사) + 일반적 관찰 (렌터카·빨래방·전력 회사의 사용량 과금). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사용량 과금의 핵심은 가격이 아니라 위험의 이동이다. 적게 쓸 위험을 고객 대신 판매자가 진다.
misconception: 사용량 과금은 고객에게 더 공정하므로 언제나 성장에 유리하다. 많이 쓰는 고객에게 더 받으니 매출도 늘어난다.

sources.text: 사용량 기반 과금(pay-per-use)의 일반적 개념. 렌터카, 빨래방, 전력 요금 등은 널리 알려진 관찰

factChecks.note: 공유 주방 계산: 시간당 $25 × 80시간 = $2,000. 손익분기 $1,200 ÷ $25 = 48시간. 신규 제빵사 10시간 × $25 = $250. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
소프트웨어 회사 월 매출(10월 $31,000, 11월 $44,000, 12월 $52,000, 1월 $27,000)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 연말 성수기 후 1월 하락이라는 패턴만 보여주려는 목적입니다.
7번 카드의 택시 미터 비유는 일반적 관찰로만 썼고 특정 연구를 인용하지 않았습니다. 연구 인용으로 바꾸려면 1차 출처를 확인하세요.
바닥 청소기 사례: 시간당 요금 = 기계 원가와 서비스 비용을 예상 사용 시간으로 나눈 값이라는 원리만 제시하고 구체 숫자는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Same pricing switch, two very different months
body: A shared kitchen and a small software company made the same change. They stopped charging a flat monthly fee and started charging for what customers actually used.
The kitchen filled its quiet hours. The software company signed up customers faster than ever, then had its slowest month in a year.

image.label: A kitchen and a laptop, each with a running meter
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 상업용 공유 주방에서 빵을 굽는 사람, 오른쪽은 노트북 화면에 이미지가 처리되는 모습. 양쪽 위에 똑같은 디지털 미터기가 숫자를 올리고 있음. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Bakers want in, but not at $1,200.
body: You run a shared commercial kitchen. Food businesses pay $1,200 a month for unlimited hours. Your regulars use about 80 hours a month.
New bakers keep touring, then leaving. They need a few hours a week and can't commit to $1,200. What do you do?

options.feedback: Newcomers can start for a few hundred dollars. But a regular at 80 hours would now pay $2,000 and may look for a cheaper kitchen.

options.text: Keep the flat fee and offer a discounted first month
options.feedback: The discount only delays the problem. A baker who needs 10 hours a month still faces $1,200 in month two.

options.text: Add a $25-an-hour option next to the membership
options.feedback: Newcomers pay only for the hours they use, and regulars keep their flat deal. Above 48 hours a month the membership is cheaper, so heavy users stay put.

cards.title: Easier to start, bumpier to run.
body: The kitchen's hourly bakers booked the empty early mornings, often starting at 10 hours ($250) a month.

The software company resizes product photos for online shops. It moved from a $500 monthly plan to $1 per 1,000 images. Small shops signed up in minutes. But revenue now rose and fell with its customers' sales.
cards.callout: After the holiday rush, shops listed fewer products, and the bill shrank with them.

cards.title: Pay-per-use
body: **Pay-per-use** means customers pay in proportion to how much they use: hours, images, miles, washes. Use little, pay little.

The real shift is about risk. With a flat fee, the customer carries the risk of paying for something they barely use. With pay-per-use, **the seller carries that risk**. That makes it easier for customers to say yes, and it makes the seller's income less predictable.

image.label: A weight labelled 'risk of low use' moving from customer to seller
image.brief: 시소 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Flat fee'에서는 'Risk of low use'라고 적힌 추가 고객 쪽에, 오른쪽 'Pay-per-use'에서는 같은 추가 판매자 쪽에 놓여 있음. 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Pick a meter that tracks value.
body: The unit you charge for matters as much as the price. A good meter rises when the customer gets more out of you.
list: **Kitchen hours:** more hours means more baking and more product to sell
**Images processed:** more images usually means the shop is listing more products
**Miles, loads, kilowatt-hours:** the long-standing meters of car hire, laundromats and power companies
cards.callout: If the meter climbs while the customer's benefit stays flat, expect complaints and cancellations.

cards.title: Best when use is uneven or uncertain.
body: Pay-per-use works when customers can't predict how much they'll need, or when use comes in bursts. A new baker doesn't know if her cakes will sell. A new online shop doesn't know its traffic.

It works less well when use is steady and heavy. Those customers often prefer a flat price they can budget for, and many will pay a little extra for that certainty. That's why the kitchen kept its membership.

cards.title: A visible meter changes behavior.
body: When people can see the meter running, some use less than they'd like, the way riders watch a taxi fare tick up. Less use can mean less value, and less reason to stay.
Your costs don't shrink with usage, either. The kitchen pays rent in quiet months too. So many businesses blend models: a small base fee plus usage, a monthly cap, or prepaid bundles of hours.

image.label: A customer nervously watching a ticking meter
image.brief: 카페 테이블 위 노트북 옆에 커다란 택시 미터기가 놓여 있고, 사람이 손을 멈춘 채 미터기 숫자를 걱정스럽게 바라봄. 따뜻하고 약간 유머러스한 톤. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now you make floor scrubbers.
body: You sell industrial floor-scrubbing machines to warehouses for $20,000 each. A large warehouse operator asks to pay per hour of scrubbing instead, with nothing upfront. Your machines already log their own hours.

options.text: Agree, with an hourly rate plus a modest monthly minimum
options.feedback: The customer gets the low-risk start they asked for, and the minimum covers part of your machine cost if their usage drops. You share the risk instead of taking all of it.

options.text: Agree, pricing each hour at the machine cost divided by expected hours
options.feedback: The math works only if they use it as much as you expect. If the warehouse slows down, you've funded a $20,000 machine that barely runs.

options.text: Decline, because metered pricing suits software, not machines
options.feedback: Equipment is often a good fit, because the meter tracks real work done. Saying no may send this customer to a rival who says yes.

cards.title: Pay-per-use moves the risk of low use onto you.
body: It lowers the barrier to starting and ties your income to your customers' success. In return, you take on their slow months.
**Try it today:** look at how much your customers use you, month to month. If it swings widely, test a usage-based option for new customers only.
